body: Albanian licence plates feature either blue strips on both sides or a unique single red strip on the left, which is exclusive to Albania in Europe.
Sky rifts from poor camera stitching are common in Albania, but are also frequently seen in Montenegro.
Albanian bollards, which are also found in Italy, have a black top with a red and grey reflector and a white bottom.
Pole tops with an upside-down triangle shape are a good clue for Albania, though similar ones exist in other Balkan countries.
Simple pole tops with horizontal bars are more indicative of Albania than Montenegro.
Albanian chevrons are white on black. While other Southern European countries use them, they help distinguish Albania from Montenegro.
The back of road signs in Albania are often painted black, a feature shared with Italy and Romania.
Albanian stop and directional signs often feature a distinct 'S' with short, angled ends. This is also seen in Italy.
Speed limit signs in Albania use a bold font, which is noticeably thinner in Montenegro.
Albania often has flat, wide guardrail endings that bend away from the road, similar to Italy.
The Albanian language is unique and recognizable by its use of special characters like Ë/ë and Ç/ç.
The Albanian word for street is 'rruga'.
Albania is a generally mountainous country with a Mediterranean climate, green mountains, and occasional flat agricultural valleys.
Exposed red soil is common in Albania, more so than in Montenegro, but similar to Greece near the border.
Cylinder-shaped water tanks on roofs are very common in Albania, distinguishing it from Montenegro.
Albanian architecture shows strong Italian influence, with pastel-coloured, blocky buildings, orange tiled roofs, and many balconies.
Mercedes is the most popular car brand in Albania, with older sedans being particularly common.
Street View coverage in Albania is limited but includes a mix of rural roads and larger towns, not just main highways.
Albanian coverage meta consists of two types: a car with a long antenna and sky rifts, or a car with a short antenna and no rifts.
Albania is mostly mountainous, especially in the north and south. The west contains low-lying flatlands, and a notable flat plateau exists around Korçë in the southeast.
The road into Theth National Park is recognizable by its tall, jagged mountains, which often have bare sides.
Along the eastern Montenegrin border, the road runs through a valley with tall, fully exposed cliff sides.
Maja e Papingut, a massive mountain in southern Albania with a near-vertical cliffside, is a prominent landmark visible from nearby roads.
A wide, mostly dried-out river valley is visible along the SH71 between Pishaj and Kokel.
The large Bay of Vlorë, recognizable by the Karaburun peninsula and Sazan island, is visible from the SH4 between Vlorë and Orikum.
Northwest of Vlorë, some roads are identifiable by a coastal-looking Aleppo pine forest.
On the SH4 between Levan and Tepelenë and near the Greek border, you might see double outer road lines with a wide gap.
Near the Greek border on the E86, you can find unique round bollards with a simple red reflector, similar to Turkish bollards.
The E86 near Lake Ohrid is one of three Albanian roads with yellow centre lines, easily recognized by the lake to the east.
The SH97, another road with yellow centre lines, runs through a hilly landscape and small valleys.
The SH1 north of Tirana, the third road with yellow centre lines, passes through a wide valley flanked by tall mountains.
The A1 highway between Fushë Milot and Thumanë is the only divided highway in Albania with a triple guardrail divider.
The SH2 (Durrës-Tirana) and SH4 (Lushnjë-Rrogozhinë) are divided by simple concrete blocks.
In Tirana, Durrës, and on the A3/SH3 south of Tirana, highways are divided by concrete blocks with grass and greenery in the middle.
The SH4 between Durrës and Fier is a non-mountainous road divided by a basic double guardrail.
The E851 is the only divided road with a basic double guardrail that goes directly through mountains.
The A2 north of Vlorë is a flat highway recognized by its double guardrail divider with an extra tall fence.
The city of Lezhë is often recognizable by the old castle on a tall hill overlooking the city.
Gjirokastër is a city situated on the western hillside of a wide valley.
